sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Brown County, Wisconsin
Green Bay Downtown Historic District (NRHP row)

stops.name: Brown County Courthouse
stops.description: Charles E. Bell's 1908 Beaux-Arts courthouse is still the working seat of Brown County, and its dome is the fixed point downtown Green Bay orients itself around.

stops.name: Kellogg Public Library
stops.description: This Classical Revival building was the first Carnegie-funded library in Wisconsin and later shared its rooms with the Neville museum, which outgrew it and crossed the river in 1983.

stops.name: Hotel Northland
stops.description: Opened in 1924 as the largest hotel in Wisconsin, it housed visiting teams on Packers weekends and put up guests from Eleanor Roosevelt to John F. Kennedy before a 44 million dollar restoration brought it back in 2019.

stops.name: Meyer Theatre
stops.description: Built in 1929 as the Fox Theatre, this Art Deco and Spanish Colonial movie palace was restored in 2002 and now seats about a thousand people for live shows.

stops.name: St. Willebrord Catholic Church
stops.description: The cornerstone of this Gothic Revival parish church went down in 1891, and it is a marked stop on the Packers Heritage Trail because Vince Lombardi attended Mass here before games.

stops.name: Christ Episcopal Church Complex
stops.description: Raised in 1899 and 1900 in Late Gothic Revival stone, the church and its 1911 rectory now serve a different congregation as the Divine Temple Church of God.

stops.name: Milwaukee Road Passenger Depot
stops.description: Charles S. Frost designed this Flemish Renaissance Revival depot in 1898; it took passengers until 1957 and reopened to the public in 2022 as the home of the Greater Green Bay Community Foundation.

stops.name: CityDeck
stops.description: A quarter mile of timber boardwalk finished in 2012 along the Fox River between the Walnut Street and Ray Nitschke bridges, with platforms that step right out over the water.

stops.name: Ray Nitschke Memorial Bridge
stops.description: Main Street crosses the Fox River on this 1998 span, named for the Packers linebacker who anchored five championship defenses in the 1960s.

stops.name: Chicago and North Western Railway Passenger Depot
stops.description: The 1899 depot in the Broadway District is where championship Packers teams were met by crowds coming home by rail, and it spent 25 years as a brewery before that tenant moved out in 2021.

stops.name: Receiver
stops.description: A 22-foot concrete receiver stretches for a catch outside the old rail depot on Donald Driver Way, repainted in 2013 to portray the Packers receiver the street is named for.

stops.name: Tarlton Theatre
stops.description: Built around 1925 as a car dealership and remade in 1941 into a Streamline Moderne cinema, it sat empty and reinvented itself repeatedly before reopening in 2018 as a theater again.

stops.name: Neville Public Museum of Brown County
stops.description: The county museum of northeast Wisconsin and the Upper Peninsula has occupied this riverbank building since 1983, and it serves as the trailhead for the Packers Heritage Trail.

note: Green Bay chosen because the rotation has run alphabetically through Detroit and Green Bay has never appeared in the nightly history. Swept the Brown County NRHP list, a Wikipedia GeoSearch of a 4 km radius around downtown (44.5133, -88.0133), and the Broadway-Walnut and Green Bay Downtown district listings. 13 stops verified individually, all still standing and in use; none lack a ZIP except three that genuinely have no street address of their own (CityDeck, the Ray Nitschke bridge, and the Receiver statue, which stands on the plaza outside 200 Dousman St). The batch is a two-bank loop: the Jefferson/Adams/Washington blocks on the east side, across the Fox on the Nitschke bridge or the CityDeck boardwalk, and back through the Broadway District. Wikipedia's infobox gives the Tarlton's address as 100 S Broadway; the theater's own contact page says 405 W Walnut St, and that is what is filed here. Dropped as outliers beyond a walkable loop: City Stadium at Green Bay East High (about 1.1 mi east, the Packers home from 1925 to 1956, a strong stop if you ever want a driving tour), Heritage Hill State Park with its four Fort Howard buildings and the Cotton and Baird houses (about 3 mi south in Allouez), Lambeau Field and the Packers Hall of Fame (about 3 mi southwest), Bay Beach Amusement Park and the Zippin Pippin coaster (about 2.5 mi northeast), and Hazelwood at 1008 S Monroe Ave (about 0.85 mi south, the closest near-miss and the one worth reconsidering if a longer loop is acceptable). Also dropped: the Green Bay YMCA at 235 N Jefferson St, which is an NRHP row with an address and coordinates but has no article of its own and I could not verify its current condition; and the historic districts themselves (Green Bay Downtown, Broadway-Dousman, Broadway-Walnut, Oakland-Dousman), which are areas rather than single places a player can stand in front of.
